name: Danny Yu
role: Software Developer · Builds internal tools for STEM education
summary: Software developer who builds the internal tools behind SFU's K-12 STEM outreach program end to end, improving them in small steps and building with scale in mind. A notes site, a Typst template, and a web-dev showcase have grown into program-wide tools: the lesson site used in class, curriculum planning, and camper-project publishing. Works mainly in Claude Code with agentic workflows, and keeps refining that workflow as AI development practices change.

skills.label: Use with AI help, learning to write unaided
skills.items: TypeScript, Astro / Hono, Cloudflare (Workers, D1, R2), Docker

skills.label: AI-assisted development
skills.items: Claude Code as a daily tool: custom skills, hooks, and subagents; taking a spec to a deployed system and owning what ships

experience.org: SFU Science Alive (Faculty of Applied Sciences Outreach)
bullets: Built *hello-wattson* as a notes site for instructors to teach from and students to keep working after events; it now serves 22 programs with built-in code editors, so students never leave the site.

Prototyped *campkit* as a Typst template to replace the unwieldy Word docs our curriculum lived in; now the single source of truth for supplies and the central place for all our events. As of Nov. 2026: 405 activities and lessons, 41 programs, six writers.
Grew *spark-gallery* from a showcase for campers' web-dev projects into a shared archive for tech, science, and engineering camps. As of Nov. 2026: 47 camps, 471 campers, and 497 projects published.
Trained and managed a team of 5 tech instructors across 26 coding and technology camps for grades 2-12 in summer 2026; authored SPARK, the program's activity-design framework.
Built a Java JSON response builder for API validation and generated Java bindings from Thrift IDLs, integrating them with Wiremock containers for test stubs.
Implemented a single source of truth for regression tests using the Trino REST API.
Wrote automated GUI tests in Java and Selenium and set up a Docker + Jenkins continuous-testing environment.

Built the human-move detection module with a Raspberry Pi camera and OpenCV, comparing board states to identify the moved piece; drove an electromagnetic trolley in Python to execute the machine's moves.
